sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between the Linux kernel and a Linux distribution?

The kernel is the core that manages memory, processes, devices and filesystems. Linux itself is only that kernel. A distribution wraps it with everything else you need to have a usable system: a package manager, an init system, shell utilities, libraries and defaults. Ubuntu, Alpine and Fedora all run the same kernel, so the differences between them are packaging, release cadence and choices such as glibc versus musl. That is why "Linux" in conversation almost always means a distribution.
Which Linux distribution should I learn for DevOps?

Ubuntu, because it is the default on most cloud providers, has the largest body of documentation, and the apt commands you learn transfer to Debian. Add familiarity with a RHEL-family system, Rocky, Alma or CentOS Stream, since regulated and enterprise environments use them and dnf, SELinux and firewalld behave differently enough to matter. Alpine is worth knowing specifically because it dominates container base images, where musl instead of glibc causes real surprises.
Do I need to learn the command line, or is a GUI enough?

The command line, without much qualification. Servers are administered over SSH with no desktop installed, container images contain no GUI, and every automation tool, Ansible, CI pipelines, shell scripts, expresses work as commands. Beyond necessity it is also the only form that is reproducible: a command can be committed to a repository, reviewed and re-run, while a sequence of clicks cannot. A graphical environment is a convenience on your own machine and absent everywhere you will actually work.
Why is Linux used for servers and containers rather than Windows?

Three reasons compound. It is free to run at scale with no per-instance licensing. It is efficient. A minimal install uses a fraction of the memory a Windows Server needs, which directly changes cloud cost. And containers are a Linux kernel feature: namespaces and cgroups are what make them possible, which is why Docker on Windows and macOS runs a Linux virtual machine underneath. The ecosystem followed, so nearly all infrastructure tooling targets Linux first.
What is a shell and how does it differ from the terminal?

The terminal is the window, the shell is the program running inside it that interprets what you type. bash is the long-standing default, zsh ships as standard on macOS, and sh is the minimal POSIX shell that Alpine and most container images provide via ash or dash. The distinction matters in practice: a script starting #!/bin/bash fails on an image with no bash, and features such as [[ ]] and arrays are bash extensions that plain sh does not support.
How much Linux do I need before learning Docker or Kubernetes?

Enough to be comfortable rather than expert: navigating the filesystem, reading and editing files, permissions and ownership, processes and signals, and following logs. Those map directly onto container work. A container is a Linux process, docker exec drops you into a shell, and most failures are permissions, a missing file or a process not listening where you expected. People who skip this find container debugging opaque, because the concepts underneath were never learned.

introduction-to-linux.markdown:
## Introduction & Overview

Learn what Linux is: kernel versus distribution versus shell, which distro to learn for DevOps, and why servers and containers overwhelmingly run Linux.

## What Is Linux?

Linux is an open source operating system family built around the Linux kernel. In simple terms, it is the software layer that helps your computer talk to hardware, manage files, run programs, and control memory, networking, and users.

Many people say “Linux” when they really mean a complete operating system such as Ubuntu or CentOS. That is common in everyday conversation, but it helps to separate the main pieces.

The kernel is the core of the operating system. It handles low-level jobs such as CPU scheduling, memory allocation, device drivers, and process management.

A distribution or distro is a complete Linux operating system built around the kernel. It bundles package managers, default tools, system services, documentation, and a release model. Ubuntu, CentOS Stream, and Alpine are all distros.

A shell is the command-line interface you use to interact with the system. Popular shells include bash, zsh, and sh. When you type commands like ls or cd, the shell reads your input and launches the right program.

Tip: A useful mental model is: kernel = engine, distro = complete car, shell = steering wheel.

## Why Linux Is Everywhere in DevOps

Most modern infrastructure runs on Linux. Cloud virtual machines, Kubernetes worker nodes, containers, CI runners, load balancers, and monitoring tools often use Linux under the hood.

DevOps engineers use Linux because it is:

If you know Linux, you can move more confidently between local development, staging, and production systems.

Imagine a team deploying a web application to AWS. Their EC2 instances run Ubuntu, their Docker containers use Alpine as a base image, and their Kubernetes control tools run on Linux in CI. Even if the developers use macOS or Windows locally, the production path still depends heavily on Linux skills.

## Common Linux Distributions

Different distros target different goals.

Ubuntu is one of the most beginner-friendly Linux distributions. It is common on cloud servers, tutorials, and developer workstations. It uses the apt package manager and has a large community.

Example package install:

CentOS Stream is closely related to Red Hat Enterprise Linux. It is often seen in enterprise environments and is useful when learning Linux administration in business settings. Red Hat style systems typically use dnf or yum.

Alpine Linux is very small and security-focused. It is especially popular in containers because of its lightweight footprint.

Note: Alpine uses musl instead of glibc, so a few binaries behave differently compared to Ubuntu or CentOS-based systems.

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx
```

## Linux on Servers, VMs, and Containers

Linux is not just for laptops. You will meet it in several forms:

In containers, Linux becomes even more important because containers rely on Linux kernel features such as namespaces and cgroups.

## GUI vs Command Line

Linux can run desktop environments with graphical interfaces, but in DevOps you often work mainly in the terminal. That is because servers are commonly accessed over SSH and automated with scripts.

A GUI is helpful for beginners, but command-line skills scale better when managing many systems.

For example, updating ten servers through a GUI would be slow. Running one script over SSH is much faster.

These commands help you quickly learn what kernel and distro you are using.

```bash
ssh devops@server1
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
```

## Why Open Source Matters

Linux is open source, which means its source code can be inspected, modified, and redistributed under open source licenses. For DevOps teams, this matters because:

Open source does not automatically mean easy, but it does mean the platform is flexible and widely shared.

## What You Should Remember

Linux is the foundation of much of modern infrastructure. The kernel is the core engine, a distribution packages the full operating system, and the shell gives you a command-line way to control it.

As a DevOps engineer, Linux knowledge helps you troubleshoot servers, automate tasks, manage containers, and understand what production systems are actually doing.

If you remember only one thing from this lesson, remember this: learning Linux is not just learning commands. It is learning how modern systems are operated.

Question: Why is Linux especially common in that kind of environment?

Pick the distribution the tutorial describes as small and common in containers.

A distribution wraps it with everything else you need to have a usable system: a package manager, an init system, shell utilities, libraries and defaults. That is why "Linux" in conversation almost always means a distribution.

Servers are administered over SSH with no desktop installed, container images contain no GUI, and every automation tool, Ansible, CI pipelines, shell scripts, expresses work as commands. Beyond necessity it is also the only form that is reproducible: a command can be committed to a repository, reviewed and re-run, while a sequence of clicks cannot. A graphical environment is a convenience on your own machine and absent everywhere you will actually work.

Three reasons compound. It is free to run at scale with no per-instance licensing. It is efficient. A minimal install uses a fraction of the memory a Windows Server needs, which directly changes cloud cost. And containers are a Linux kernel feature: namespaces and cgroups are what make them possible, which is why Docker on Windows and macOS runs a Linux virtual machine underneath. The ecosystem followed, so nearly all infrastructure tooling targets Linux first.

The terminal is the window, the shell is the program running inside it that interprets what you type. bash is the long-standing default, zsh ships as standard on macOS, and sh is the minimal POSIX shell that Alpine and most container images provide via ash or dash. The distinction matters in practice: a script starting #!/bin/bash fails on an image with no bash, and features such as [[ ]] and arrays are bash extensions that plain sh does not support.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard?

A specification defining what each top-level directory is for, which is why /etc holds configuration on Ubuntu, Alpine and Fedora alike. It means knowledge transfers between distributions and tooling can make safe assumptions about where things live. Compliance is not absolute. Distributions differ in details, and several have merged /bin into /usr/bin via symlinks, but the broad structure is dependable enough to navigate an unfamiliar system.
What is the difference between /etc, /var and /usr?

/etc holds system-wide configuration: text files you edit, and the first place to look when changing how something behaves. /var holds variable data the system writes during operation. Logs in /var/log, databases and container images in /var/lib, queued mail and print jobs in /var/spool, and it is what grows. /usr holds installed programs and their static supporting files, managed by the package manager and not normally edited by hand.
What is the difference between /tmp and /var/tmp?

/tmp is for short-lived files and is cleared on reboot, and on many modern systems it is a tmpfs living in RAM, which means writing a large file there consumes memory and disappears entirely on restart. /var/tmp is also temporary but is expected to survive a reboot, making it the right choice for a long-running job's intermediate files. Both are world-writable with the sticky bit set, so users cannot delete each other's files.
What are /proc and /sys?

Virtual filesystems that expose kernel state as readable files, occupying no disk space at all. /proc is mostly per-process information, /proc/<pid>/ describes a running process, plus system-wide values such as /proc/meminfo and /proc/cpuinfo. /sys exposes devices and kernel parameters, and writing to files there changes settings at runtime. This is why commands like free and ps work: they read and format these files rather than asking the kernel through a special interface.
Where should I install software that does not come from a package?

/opt for a self-contained third-party application that keeps its own directory tree, and /usr/local when you are installing something that follows the usual bin, lib, share layout, /usr/local/bin is on PATH by default and is the conventional place for a compiled binary. Avoid writing into /usr/bin yourself, because that belongs to the package manager and your file will eventually be overwritten or conflict with an upgrade.
Which directories should I check first when a disk fills up?

/var/log and /var/lib, in that order. Logs grow without limit when rotation is missing or misconfigured, and /var/lib/docker or /var/lib/containerd accumulates images, layers and volumes surprisingly fast on a build host. sudo du -sh /var/* | sort -h narrows it in one command. If df reports a full disk but du does not account for it, look for a deleted file still held open by a process with sudo lsof +L1.

linux-filesystem.markdown:
## Understanding the Linux Filesystem

One of the biggest mindset shifts for beginners is that Linux does not organize storage around drive letters like `C:` or `D:`. Instead, everything starts from a single top-level directory called the **root directory**, written as `/`.

Files, folders, devices, and even process information appear somewhere under that root. This design makes Linux systems predictable once you learn the layout.

## What Is the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard?

The **Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)** is a convention that describes where different types of files should live on Unix-like systems. Not every distribution follows it perfectly, but most of them follow the general structure.

The goal is consistency. If configuration files are usually in `/etc` and logs are usually in `/var/log`, administrators do not have to guess where important data is stored.

> **Tip:** Memorizing a few key directories saves time when troubleshooting a server over SSH.

## The Root Directory `/`

The **root directory** is the top of the filesystem tree. Every path begins from here.

For example:

```bash
/etc/ssh/sshd_config
/var/log/syslog
/home/devops/.bashrc
```

Do not confuse `/` with the **root user**. The slash is the top directory. The root user is the superuser account with administrative power.

## Important Linux Directories

### `/etc`

`/etc` stores system-wide **configuration files**. You will often edit files here when managing services, users, networking, or security.

Examples:

```bash
/etc/hosts
/etc/passwd
/etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

In DevOps, `/etc` matters because many service settings are plain text and easy to automate.

### `/var`

`/var` holds **variable data** that changes over time. This includes logs, caches, spool files, and application state.

Common examples:

```bash
/var/log/
/var/lib/
/var/cache/
```

When a service fails, logs in `/var/log` are usually one of the first places to check.

### `/tmp`

`/tmp` is used for **temporary files**. Applications often write short-lived data here. On many systems, its contents may be cleaned automatically.

You should never store important long-term files in `/tmp`.

> **Note:** In operations work, a missing file in `/tmp` is often expected because cleanup jobs may remove old temporary data.

### `/home`

`/home` stores personal directories for regular users.

Example:

```bash
/home/alex
/home/devops
```

A userâs shell profile, SSH keys, and personal scripts are often stored here.

### `/usr`

`/usr` contains many user-space programs, libraries, and documentation. Despite its name, it is not only for user home data.

Common subdirectories include:

- `/usr/bin` for commands
- `/usr/sbin` for admin commands
- `/usr/lib` for libraries
- `/usr/share` for shared data and docs

### `/proc`

`/proc` is a **virtual filesystem** that exposes kernel and process information. Files here are generated dynamically by the system rather than stored like normal files.

Useful examples:

```bash
cat /proc/cpuinfo
cat /proc/meminfo
cat /proc/1/status
```

This directory is valuable when diagnosing performance or understanding system state.

## Absolute vs Relative Paths

A **path** tells Linux where a file or directory is located.

### Absolute Paths

An **absolute path** starts with `/` and gives the full location from the root directory.

Example:

```bash
/home/devops/projects/app/config.yaml
```

No matter where you currently are in the shell, that path points to the same file.

### Relative Paths

A **relative path** starts from your current working directory.

If you are in `/home/devops/projects`, then:

```bash
cd app
cat config.yaml
```

Here, `app` and `config.yaml` are relative paths.

### Special Path Shortcuts

Linux also uses a few path shortcuts:

- `.` means the current directory
- `..` means the parent directory
- `~` usually means your home directory

Example:

```bash
cd ~/projects
ls ../
```

## Reading the Filesystem Like a DevOps Engineer

Suppose an Nginx service fails. A practical workflow might look like this:

```bash
cd /etc/nginx
ls
cat nginx.conf
cd /var/log/nginx
tail -n 20 error.log
```

This simple flow uses two key areas of the filesystem: configuration in `/etc` and logs in `/var/log`.

Another example is user troubleshooting:

```bash
cat /etc/passwd
ls /home
```

These commands help you see registered users and their home directories.

## Why Filesystem Knowledge Matters

Filesystem knowledge is not trivia. It directly improves troubleshooting speed.

When you know where things usually live, you can:

- find config files faster
- inspect logs without guessing
- understand application layouts
- write better automation scripts
- avoid dangerous mistakes like deleting the wrong path

Beginners often struggle because Linux feels unfamiliar. The fix is repetition: navigate, inspect, and connect each directory to a real use case.

    title: 'Exercise 3: Spotting a relative path',

    description: 'Determine which example path depends on the current working directory.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: '/home/devops/projects/app/config.yaml' },

      { id: 'b', text: '/etc/ssh/sshd_config' },

      { id: 'c', text: '/var/log/syslog' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'app/config.yaml' },

    ],

    correctId: 'd',

    explanation: 'A relative path does not begin with /. The tutorial uses examples like app and config.yaml to show paths that are resolved from your current working directory.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: 'This is an absolute path because it starts at the root directory with /. It points to the same file no matter where you currently are.',

      b: 'Because it begins with /, this is also absolute and independent of the current directory.',

      c: 'This path is absolute as well. The leading slash tells Linux to resolve it from the filesystem root.',

    },

  }}
/>

---

## Key takeaways

- **Everything hangs off `/`.** There are no drive letters; additional disks are mounted into the tree.
- **`/etc` is configuration, `/var` is changing data, `/usr` is installed software.** That split explains most of the layout.
- **`/tmp` may be cleared on reboot** and is often a tmpfs in RAM; `/var/tmp` persists.
- **`/proc` and `/sys` are not on disk**: they are kernel interfaces presented as files.
- **`/var/log` and `/var/lib` are what fill a disk**, so check them first.
- **`/opt` and `/usr/local` are for software outside the package manager**; leave `/usr/bin` to it.
- **A file starting with `.` is hidden only by convention**: `ls -a` shows it.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard?**

A specification defining what each top-level directory is for, which is why `/etc` holds configuration on Ubuntu, Alpine and Fedora alike. It means knowledge transfers between distributions and tooling can make safe assumptions about where things live. Compliance is not absolute. Distributions differ in details, and several have merged `/bin` into `/usr/bin` via symlinks, but the broad structure is dependable enough to navigate an unfamiliar system.

**What is the difference between /etc, /var and /usr?**

`/etc` holds system-wide configuration: text files you edit, and the first place to look when changing how something behaves. `/var` holds variable data the system writes during operation. Logs in `/var/log`, databases and container images in `/var/lib`, queued mail and print jobs in `/var/spool`, and it is what grows. `/usr` holds installed programs and their static supporting files, managed by the package manager and not normally edited by hand.

**What is the difference between /tmp and /var/tmp?**

`/tmp` is for short-lived files and is cleared on reboot, and on many modern systems it is a tmpfs living in RAM, which means writing a large file there consumes memory and disappears entirely on restart. `/var/tmp` is also temporary but is expected to survive a reboot, making it the right choice for a long-running job's intermediate files. Both are world-writable with the sticky bit set, so users cannot delete each other's files.

**What are /proc and /sys?**

Virtual filesystems that expose kernel state as readable files, occupying no disk space at all. `/proc` is mostly per-process information, `/proc/<pid>/` describes a running process, plus system-wide values such as `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/cpuinfo`. `/sys` exposes devices and kernel parameters, and writing to files there changes settings at runtime. This is why commands like `free` and `ps` work: they read and format these files rather than asking the kernel through a special interface.

**Where should I install software that does not come from a package?**

`/opt` for a self-contained third-party application that keeps its own directory tree, and `/usr/local` when you are installing something that follows the usual `bin`, `lib`, `share` layout, `/usr/local/bin` is on `PATH` by default and is the conventional place for a compiled binary. Avoid writing into `/usr/bin` yourself, because that belongs to the package manager and your file will eventually be overwritten or conflict with an upgrade.

**Which directories should I check first when a disk fills up?**

`/var/log` and `/var/lib`, in that order. Logs grow without limit when rotation is missing or misconfigured, and `/var/lib/docker` or `/var/lib/containerd` accumulates images, layers and volumes surprisingly fast on a build host. `sudo du -sh /var/* | sort -h` narrows it in one command. If `df` reports a full disk but `du` does not account for it, look for a deleted file still held open by a process with `sudo lsof +L1`.

linux-navigation.markdown:
## Why Navigation Skills Matter

Before you can manage files, edit configs, or inspect logs, you need to know where you are and how to move around. Linux navigation commands are simple, but they form the foundation of almost every admin or DevOps task.

A common production workflow might involve jumping from a service config in `/etc`, to a binary in `/usr/bin`, to logs in `/var/log`, all within a few minutes.

## Finding Your Current Location with `pwd`

The `pwd` command means **print working directory**. It shows your current location in the filesystem.

```bash
pwd
/home/devops/projects/api
```

This matters because many commands use relative paths. If you are in the wrong directory, the same command may fail or affect the wrong file.

## Listing Files with `ls`

The `ls` command lists directory contents.

```bash
ls
ls -l
ls -la
ls -lh
```

Useful flags:

- `-l` shows a long listing format
- `-a` includes hidden files like `.bashrc`
- `-h` shows readable sizes such as `4K` or `12M`

Example:

```bash
ls -lah /etc/nginx
```

This shows permissions, owners, sizes, and hidden entries inside `/etc/nginx`.

> **Tip:** Hidden files in Linux usually start with a dot, such as `.gitignore` or `.env`.

## Changing Directories with `cd`

The `cd` command means **change directory**.

```bash
cd /var/log
cd ..
cd ~
cd -
```

Useful patterns:

- `cd ..` goes up one level
- `cd ~` goes to your home directory
- `cd -` returns to the previous directory

A real example:

```bash
cd /etc
cd nginx
cd ../ssh
```

This is faster than typing every full path from scratch.

## Visualizing Structure with `tree`

The `tree` command shows a directory as a tree structure.

```bash
tree
tree -L 2 /etc
```

`-L 2` limits output to two levels deep, which keeps things readable.

If `tree` is not installed on a system, that is normal. Many minimal servers do not include it by default.

## Identifying File Types with `file`

The `file` command tells you what a file actually is.

```bash
file /bin/bash
file /etc/hosts
file app.tar.gz
```

This is helpful when extensions are missing or misleading. A file called `backup` could be plain text, a gzip archive, or a binary.

## Locating Commands with `which` and `whereis`

`which` shows the executable path that your shell will run.

```bash
which bash
which python3
```

Example output:

```bash
/usr/bin/bash
```

`whereis` looks more broadly for a commandâs binary, source, and manual pages.

```bash
whereis bash
whereis ssh
```

Use `which` when you want the exact command path the shell uses. Use `whereis` when you want extra related locations.

## Reading Documentation with `man`

The `man` command opens **manual pages**.

```bash
man ls
man chmod
```

Manual pages explain syntax, options, and behavior. They are one of the best ways to learn Linux directly from the system.

Search inside a man page by typing `/pattern` and press `q` to quit.

> **Note:** Some containers and tiny images do not include man pages to save space.

## Using Built-In Help with `help`

The `help` command explains shell built-ins.

```bash
help cd
help pwd
```

This is different from `man`. Commands like `cd` are often shell built-ins, so `help` may be more accurate than `man` for them.

## A Small Hands-On Workflow

Imagine you need to inspect an application directory:

```bash
pwd
ls -lah
cd /opt/myapp
tree -L 2
file deploy.sh
which bash
man grep
```

This workflow answers several questions quickly:

- where am I?
- what files are here?
- what is the directory structure?
- what type of file is this?
- which shell binary will run?
- where can I learn more about a command?

## Common Beginner Mistakes

### Forgetting the Current Directory

Running `rm config.yaml` is risky if you are not sure where you are. Use `pwd` first.

### Ignoring Hidden Files

Beginners often use `ls` and assume nothing else exists. But `.env`, `.ssh`, and `.git` are hidden unless you include `-a`.

### Not Reading Built-In Docs

Guessing flags is slower than using `man` or `help`. Linux rewards curiosity.

## Test Your Understanding

### Exercise 1: Listing hidden entries

**Scenario:** You suspect a directory contains .env and .bashrc files that plain ls does not show.

**Question:** Which command flag from the lesson should you add?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-navigation-q1',

    title: 'Exercise 1: Listing hidden entries',

    description: 'Choose the ls option that reveals dotfiles and other hidden entries.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: '-a' },

      { id: 'b', text: '-t' },

      { id: 'c', text: '-r' },

      { id: 'd', text: '-s' },

    ],

    correctId: 'a',

    explanation: 'The tutorial explains that ls -a includes hidden files whose names begin with a dot. That is why it is the right tool when important entries like .git or .env are missing from a normal listing.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      b: '-t changes sorting behavior by time, but it does not reveal hidden files.',

      c: '-r reverses sort order. It does not include dotfiles on its own.',

      d: '-s is not the flag the lesson introduced for hidden entries. The tutorial specifically pointed to -a.',

    },

  }}
/>

### Exercise 2: Choosing which versus whereis

**Question:** If you want the exact executable path your shell will run for python3, which command is the best fit?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-navigation-q2',

    title: 'Exercise 2: Choosing which versus whereis',

    description: 'Pick the command that shows the executable path your shell will use.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'whereis python3' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'tree python3' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'which python3' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'file python3' },

    ],

    correctId: 'c',

    explanation: 'The lesson distinguishes which from whereis: which shows the executable path the shell will actually run. That makes it the most precise choice when you want the command path in use.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: 'whereis searches more broadly for binaries, source, and manuals, but it is not the most exact answer for what the shell will execute.',

      b: 'tree visualizes directories. It does not resolve commands in your PATH.',

      d: 'file identifies file types, not which executable location your shell will choose.',

    },

  }}
/>

### Exercise 3: Getting help for built-ins

**Question:** Why did the tutorial recommend help cd instead of relying only on man cd?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-navigation-q3',

    title: 'Exercise 3: Getting help for built-ins',

    description: 'Identify why the help command can be more accurate for cd.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'Because help edits the current directory for you.' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'Because cd is usually a shell built-in, so help can describe it more directly.' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'Because man pages cannot exist on Linux systems.' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'Because help shows file permissions instead of documentation.' },

    ],

    correctId: 'b',

    explanation: 'The tutorial notes that commands like cd are often built into the shell rather than separate executables. In those cases, help can be the most direct and accurate documentation source.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: 'help only explains built-ins. It does not perform navigation actions for you.',

      c: 'Linux absolutely can have man pages. The point was that help is sometimes better for shell built-ins, not that man is impossible.',

      d: 'Displaying permissions is the job of tools like ls -l, not help.',

    },

  }}
/>

---

## Key takeaways

- **`pwd` when lost, `cd -` to jump back** to the previous directory.
- **`ls -lah` is the one to memorise**: long format, hidden files, human-readable sizes.
- **An absolute path starts with `/`; a relative one does not.** Scripts should use absolute.
- **`~` is your home directory**, and `~user` is someone else's.
- **Tab completion is not a convenience, it is error prevention**: it cannot complete a path that does not exist.
- **`which` finds a command on `PATH`; `type` also reveals aliases and shell builtins.**
- **`man` searches with `/`, navigates with `n`, and quits with `q`**: the same keys as `less`.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?**

An absolute path starts at the root and is unambiguous wherever you run it, `/var/log/nginx/access.log`. A relative path is interpreted from your current directory, so `logs/access.log` means something different depending on where you are. Relative paths are fine when typing interactively; use absolute paths in scripts, cron jobs and systemd units, because those run from a working directory you did not choose and "file not found" for a path that plainly exists is nearly always this.

**What do the columns in ls -l mean?**

Left to right: the permission string, link count, owner, group, size in bytes, modification time, and name. The permission string's first character is the file type, `-` for a regular file, `d` for a directory, `l` for a symlink, followed by three groups of `rwx` for user, group and other. Add `-h` for human-readable sizes and `-a` to include hidden files, which is why `ls -lah` is the form worth committing to muscle memory.

**What does cd - do?**

Returns you to the previous directory, toggling between two locations. Invaluable when moving repeatedly between a config directory and a log directory. `cd` with no argument goes home, and `cd ..` goes up one level. For deeper movement, `pushd` and `popd` maintain a stack of directories, and `dirs -v` lists it. Most of the time `cd -` plus tab completion covers everything you need.

**What is the difference between which, whereis and type?**

`which` searches your `PATH` and prints the executable that would run. `whereis` additionally locates the binary, source and man page from a system database. `type` is a shell builtin and the most informative, because it reveals things `which` cannot see. Whether the name is an alias, a shell function, or a builtin. When `which python` says one thing and the command behaves like another, `type python` explains why.

**How do I read a man page effectively?**

Man pages open in `less`, so `/pattern` searches, `n` and `N` move between matches, `g` and `G` jump to start and end, and `q` quits. Rather than reading top to bottom, search for the flag you care about, `/--exclude`, since the options section is where the answers are. `man -k <keyword>` searches all page descriptions when you do not know the command name. `tldr` is worth installing for a short page of practical examples instead of the full reference.

**Why does my terminal say "command not found" for a program I installed?**

The program is not in a directory on your `PATH`. Check with `echo $PATH` and confirm where it actually landed using `ls /usr/local/bin` or `find / -name <program> 2>/dev/null`. Fix it by adding the directory in `~/.bashrc` with `export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tool/bin"`, then opening a new shell or running `source ~/.bashrc`. The other common cause is installing with a package manager whose install location is not on `PATH`, such as a user-level `pip install` putting binaries in `~/.local/bin`.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Copy, move, delete and read files safely on Linux: why rm has no undo, cp -r versus cp -a, the trailing-slash trap, find by name and size, less versus tail.

sections.title: Working with Files Safely
paragraphs: Linux gives you powerful file commands, but power requires care. A single rm -r in the wrong location can remove important data. The good news is that the core file operations are consistent and easy to learn once you practice them.
This lesson covers the commands you will use constantly in development, troubleshooting, and server administration.

sections.title: Creating Files and Directories
paragraphs: Use mkdir to create directories.
The -p flag creates parent directories as needed and does not fail if parts already exist.
Use touch to create an empty file or update a file’s timestamp.
Tip: mkdir -p is very common in automation because it is safe for repeated runs.

sections.title: Copying Files with cp
paragraphs: The cp command copies files or directories.
A common admin pattern is to back up a config before editing it:

codeBlock.code:
cp app.conf app.conf.bak
cp -r site/ site-backup/
cp -v *.log archive/

sections.title: Moving and Renaming with mv
paragraphs: The mv command moves or renames files.
If the target is a directory, the file is moved into it. If the target is a new filename in the same directory, the file is renamed.

codeBlock.code:
mv draft.txt final.txt
mv report.txt docs/

sections.title: Removing with rm
paragraphs: The rm command deletes files. It does not move them to a recycle bin.
Note: Many production mistakes start with removing the wrong path. Double-check with pwd and ls before destructive commands.

codeBlock.code:
rm old.log
rm -r old-directory
rm -i important.txt

sections.title: Reading File Content
paragraphs: cat prints a file’s full contents.
It is best for small files.
head shows the first lines of a file.
tail shows the last lines of a file.
tail -f is especially useful for watching logs as new entries appear.
less lets you scroll through file contents interactively.
Use the arrow keys or page navigation, type /error to search, and press q to quit.

sections.title: Links: Hard Links and Symbolic Links
paragraphs: The ln command creates links.
A hard link is another directory entry that points to the same underlying file data.
Both names refer to the same inode. Deleting one name does not remove the data as long as another hard link still exists.
A symbolic link or soft link points to another path.
Symbolic links are more flexible because they can point across filesystems and to directories.
Tip: In DevOps, symbolic links are often used for versioned deployments, like linking current to the active release directory.

sections.title: A Practical Example
paragraphs: Suppose you are preparing a simple app directory:
You created a structure, added a file, made a backup, renamed it, and created a symbolic link.

codeBlock.code:
mkdir -p myapp/{config,logs,bin}
touch myapp/config/app.conf
cp myapp/config/app.conf myapp/config/app.conf.bak
mv myapp/config/app.conf.bak myapp/config/app.conf.old
ln -s myapp/logs latest-logs

sections.title: Choosing the Right Command
paragraphs: Beginners often overuse cat for huge logs. On large files, less or tail is usually better.

sections.title: Test Your Understanding
paragraphs: Question: Which command from the lesson creates project/config/environments in one step without failing if parent directories are missing?
Choose the mkdir form that safely creates nested parent directories.
Scenario: You want to watch new Nginx access log lines appear during troubleshooting.
Question: Which command is the best match?
Identify the command that continues showing new lines added to a log file.
Question: Why would ln -s be a good fit for a current release directory in a deployment?
Choose the reason symbolic links are useful in versioned deployments.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Is there any way to undo rm in Linux?

Not for practical purposes. rm unlinks the file immediately with no trash directory, and while the blocks may survive on disk until overwritten, recovery tools such as extundelete or testdisk are unreliable on a mounted filesystem and rarely worth attempting. Prevention is the whole answer: alias rm to rm -i for interactive confirmation, use a trash utility such as trash-cli for interactive work, and keep backups. Before any rm -rf, read the path out loud. Most accidents are a stray space or an unquoted variable.
What is the difference between cp -r and cp -a?

-r copies a directory recursively but resets ownership to you and updates timestamps to now. -a (archive) preserves permissions, ownership, timestamps and symlinks, which is what you want when copying system files, a web root, or anything where metadata matters. A common symptom of using -r is a service refusing to start after a copy because files it needs are now owned by the wrong user. When in doubt on system files, use -a.
Why did cp put my files in the wrong place?

Almost always the trailing slash on the source. cp -a dir dest/ copies the directory itself, producing dest/dir; cp -a dir/. dest/ copies its contents into dest. rsync has the same distinction, where rsync -a src/ dest/ syncs contents and rsync -a src dest/ creates dest/src. The other cause is a destination that does not exist, in which case cp treats the last argument as a new filename rather than a directory.
How do I find files by name or size?

find /path -name "*.log" matches by name, -iname case-insensitively, and -type f restricts to regular files. find /var -size +100M finds large files, and -mtime -7 those modified in the last week. Combine with -exec to act on results, find . -name "*.tmp" -delete, but always run the find alone first to see what it matches, because -delete and -exec rm are as unforgiving as rm itself. For searching contents rather than names, use grep -r or rg.
What is the difference between cat, less, head and tail?

cat prints the whole file to your terminal, which is fine for something small and unhelpful for a 2 GB log. less pages through it without loading it all, supports / to search, and is the right default for anything large. head -n 20 shows the first lines and tail -n 50 the last, and tail -F follows a file as it grows, surviving log rotation, which the plain -f does not.
How do I create a file or directory tree in one command?

touch file.txt creates an empty file or updates an existing one's timestamp. mkdir -p a/b/c creates the whole path, creating parents as needed and succeeding silently if it already exists, which is what makes it safe in scripts, where plain mkdir errors on an existing directory. Brace expansion handles several at once: mkdir -p project/{src,tests,docs} creates all three subdirectories in one go.

linux-file-operations.markdown:
## Working with Files Safely

Linux gives you powerful file commands, but power requires care. A single `rm -r` in the wrong location can remove important data. The good news is that the core file operations are consistent and easy to learn once you practice them.

This lesson covers the commands you will use constantly in development, troubleshooting, and server administration.

## Creating Files and Directories

Use `mkdir` to create directories.

```bash
mkdir project
mkdir -p project/config/environments
```

The `-p` flag creates parent directories as needed and does not fail if parts already exist.

Use `touch` to create an empty file or update a fileâs timestamp.

```bash
touch notes.txt
touch app.log
```

> **Tip:** `mkdir -p` is very common in automation because it is safe for repeated runs.

## Copying Files with `cp`

The `cp` command copies files or directories.

```bash
cp app.conf app.conf.bak
cp -r site/ site-backup/
cp -v *.log archive/
```

Useful flags:

- `-r` copies directories recursively
- `-v` shows what is being copied

A common admin pattern is to back up a config before editing it:

```bash
sudo cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak
```

## Moving and Renaming with `mv`

The `mv` command moves or renames files.

```bash
mv draft.txt final.txt
mv report.txt docs/
```

If the target is a directory, the file is moved into it. If the target is a new filename in the same directory, the file is renamed.

## Removing with `rm`

The `rm` command deletes files. It does not move them to a recycle bin.

```bash
rm old.log
rm -r old-directory
rm -i important.txt
```

Useful flags:

- `-r` removes directories recursively
- `-i` asks for confirmation

> **Note:** Many production mistakes start with removing the wrong path. Double-check with `pwd` and `ls` before destructive commands.

## Reading File Content

### `cat`

`cat` prints a fileâs full contents.

```bash
cat /etc/hosts
cat app.log
```

It is best for small files.

### `head`

`head` shows the first lines of a file.

```bash
head app.log
head -n 20 app.log
```

### `tail`

`tail` shows the last lines of a file.

```bash
tail app.log
tail -n 50 app.log
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
```

`tail -f` is especially useful for watching logs as new entries appear.

### `less`

`less` lets you scroll through file contents interactively.

```bash
less /var/log/syslog
```

Use the arrow keys or page navigation, type `/error` to search, and press `q` to quit.

## Links: Hard Links and Symbolic Links

The `ln` command creates links.

### Hard Links

A **hard link** is another directory entry that points to the same underlying file data.

```bash
ln original.txt hardlink.txt
```

Both names refer to the same inode. Deleting one name does not remove the data as long as another hard link still exists.

### Symbolic Links

A **symbolic link** or **soft link** points to another path.

```bash
ln -s /var/log/nginx/access.log access-current.log
```

Symbolic links are more flexible because they can point across filesystems and to directories.

> **Tip:** In DevOps, symbolic links are often used for versioned deployments, like linking `current` to the active release directory.

## A Practical Example

Suppose you are preparing a simple app directory:

```bash
mkdir -p myapp/{config,logs,bin}
touch myapp/config/app.conf
cp myapp/config/app.conf myapp/config/app.conf.bak
mv myapp/config/app.conf.bak myapp/config/app.conf.old
ln -s myapp/logs latest-logs
```

You created a structure, added a file, made a backup, renamed it, and created a symbolic link.

## Choosing the Right Command

- Use `cp` when you need a duplicate
- Use `mv` when you want to rename or relocate
- Use `rm` when you are sure you want permanent removal
- Use `cat`, `head`, `tail`, or `less` depending on file size and what part you need
- Use `ln -s` when you want a flexible pointer to another path

Beginners often overuse `cat` for huge logs. On large files, `less` or `tail` is usually better.

## Test Your Understanding

### Exercise 1: Creating directory trees

**Question:** Which command from the lesson creates project/config/environments in one step without failing if parent directories are missing?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-file-operations-q1',

    title: 'Exercise 1: Creating directory trees',

    description: 'Choose the mkdir form that safely creates nested parent directories.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'mkdir -p project/config/environments' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'touch -p project/config/environments' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'cp -r project/config/environments' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'rm -r project/config/environments' },

    ],

    correctId: 'a',

    explanation: 'The lesson highlights mkdir -p as the safe automation-friendly way to build nested directory structures. It creates any missing parent directories and does not complain if parts of the path already exist.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      b: 'touch creates files or updates timestamps. It does not build a nested directory tree.',

      c: 'cp -r copies existing directories. It does not create a new hierarchy from nothing.',

      d: 'rm -r removes directories rather than creating them.',

    },

  }}
/>

### Exercise 2: Following a growing file

**Scenario:** You want to watch new Nginx access log lines appear during troubleshooting.

**Question:** Which command is the best match?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-file-operations-q2',

    title: 'Exercise 2: Following a growing file',

    description: 'Identify the command that continues showing new lines added to a log file.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'head -n 50 /var/log/nginx/access.log' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'cat /var/log/nginx/access.log' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'touch /var/log/nginx/access.log' },

    ],

    correctId: 'c',

    explanation: 'The tutorial calls out tail -f as the tool for following a log as new entries are appended. That live view is what makes it so useful during active debugging.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: 'head shows the beginning of a file once. It does not continue tracking appended lines.',

      b: 'cat prints the current contents and exits. It is fine for small files, but it does not follow updates.',

      d: 'touch creates a file or updates its timestamp. It does not display log content at all.',

    },

  }}
/>

### Exercise 3: Using flexible links

**Question:** Why would ln -s be a good fit for a current release directory in a deployment?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-file-operations-q3',

    title: 'Exercise 3: Using flexible links',

    description: 'Choose the reason symbolic links are useful in versioned deployments.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'A symbolic link stores a full duplicate copy of the target data.' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'A symbolic link points to another path, so current can be switched to a different release directory easily.' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'A symbolic link can only point to regular files in the same filesystem.' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'A symbolic link permanently merges two directories together.' },

    ],

    correctId: 'b',

    explanation: 'The tutorial explains that symbolic links are flexible path references and are often used to point current at the active release. Changing the link can redirect users to a new release without moving all the files.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: 'That would describe copying, not linking. A symlink references a path instead of duplicating file content.',

      c: 'The lesson specifically notes that symbolic links can point across filesystems and to directories, so this restriction is incorrect.',

      d: 'Symlinks do not merge directories. They simply provide a path that resolves to another location.',

    },

  }}
/>

---

## Key takeaways

- **`rm` has no undo and no trash.** There is no recovery for an ordinary file.
- **`cp -r` for directories, `cp -a` to preserve permissions, ownership and timestamps.**
- **A trailing slash changes `cp` and `rsync` behaviour**: `dir` copies the directory, `dir/` copies its contents.
- **`mv` renames and moves** with the same command; there is no separate rename.
- **Use `rm -i` or an alias for interactive deletion** rather than trusting yourself with `-rf`.
- **`less` over `cat` for large files**, and `tail -F` for one still being written.
- **`find -exec` is powerful and unforgiving.** Run it with `-print` first to see what it matches.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is there any way to undo rm in Linux?**

Not for practical purposes. `rm` unlinks the file immediately with no trash directory, and while the blocks may survive on disk until overwritten, recovery tools such as `extundelete` or `testdisk` are unreliable on a mounted filesystem and rarely worth attempting. Prevention is the whole answer: alias `rm` to `rm -i` for interactive confirmation, use a trash utility such as `trash-cli` for interactive work, and keep backups. Before any `rm -rf`, read the path out loud. Most accidents are a stray space or an unquoted variable.

**What is the difference between cp -r and cp -a?**

`-r` copies a directory recursively but resets ownership to you and updates timestamps to now. `-a` (archive) preserves permissions, ownership, timestamps and symlinks, which is what you want when copying system files, a web root, or anything where metadata matters. A common symptom of using `-r` is a service refusing to start after a copy because files it needs are now owned by the wrong user. When in doubt on system files, use `-a`.

**Why did cp put my files in the wrong place?**

Almost always the trailing slash on the source. `cp -a dir dest/` copies the directory itself, producing `dest/dir`; `cp -a dir/. dest/` copies its *contents* into `dest`. `rsync` has the same distinction, where `rsync -a src/ dest/` syncs contents and `rsync -a src dest/` creates `dest/src`. The other cause is a destination that does not exist, in which case `cp` treats the last argument as a new filename rather than a directory.

**How do I find files by name or size?**

`find /path -name "*.log"` matches by name, `-iname` case-insensitively, and `-type f` restricts to regular files. `find /var -size +100M` finds large files, and `-mtime -7` those modified in the last week. Combine with `-exec` to act on results, `find . -name "*.tmp" -delete`, but always run the `find` alone first to see what it matches, because `-delete` and `-exec rm` are as unforgiving as `rm` itself. For searching *contents* rather than names, use `grep -r` or `rg`.

**What is the difference between cat, less, head and tail?**

`cat` prints the whole file to your terminal, which is fine for something small and unhelpful for a 2 GB log. `less` pages through it without loading it all, supports `/` to search, and is the right default for anything large. `head -n 20` shows the first lines and `tail -n 50` the last, and `tail -F` follows a file as it grows, surviving log rotation, which the plain `-f` does not.

**How do I create a file or directory tree in one command?**

`touch file.txt` creates an empty file or updates an existing one's timestamp. `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates the whole path, creating parents as needed and succeeding silently if it already exists, which is what makes it safe in scripts, where plain `mkdir` errors on an existing directory. Brace expansion handles several at once: `mkdir -p project/{src,tests,docs}` creates all three subdirectories in one go.

paragraphs: When should I use grep, sed or awk?

grep selects lines matching a pattern and does nothing else. Reach for it when the question is "which lines". sed is a stream editor for substitution and deletion, so "change this to that" is its job, usually sed 's/old/new/g'. awk splits each line into fields and can do arithmetic and conditionals, so it wins whenever you care about columns, awk '$3 > 100 {print $1}'. If you find yourself building something with three pipes and a conditional, that is usually one awk program.
How do I replace text in a file from the command line?

sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt, -i edits in place, s substitutes, and g replaces every occurrence on each line rather than just the first. There is one portability trap: GNU sed on Linux accepts bare -i, while BSD sed on macOS requires a backup suffix, so the same command needs sed -i '' 's/old/new/g' there. Scripts that must run on both should use perl -pi -e 's/old/new/g', which behaves identically everywhere.
What is the difference between cut and awk for extracting columns?

cut -d' ' -f3 treats every single delimiter as a boundary, so two consecutive spaces produce an empty field, which makes it unreliable on command output aligned with variable whitespace. awk '{print $3}' treats any run of whitespace as one separator by default, which is almost always what you want for ps, df or log output. cut is the better tool for genuinely delimited data such as CSV or /etc/passwd, where the delimiter is exactly one character.
How do I count unique occurrences in a log file?

sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn | head. The first sort is mandatory, because uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates and silently does nothing otherwise, that is the most common mistake with it. uniq -c prefixes each line with its count, and sort -rn orders by that count descending. Combined with awk to pull out a field, it answers most log questions: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head gives your top client IPs.
How do I search recursively through a directory?

grep -rn "pattern" ., r recurses, n adds line numbers so the output is actionable. Add -i for case-insensitive and --include="*.py" to limit by file type. grep -rl lists only the matching filenames, which is what you want when feeding results into another command. For large repositories, ripgrep (rg) is considerably faster and respects .gitignore by default, which usually removes more noise than any set of --exclude flags.
Why does my error message disappear when I pipe a command?

Because a pipe carries stdout only, and errors go to stderr. command | grep error therefore filters the normal output and lets the actual error print straight to your terminal, unfiltered. Redirect stderr into stdout first with command 2>&1 | grep error. The order matters: 2>&1 >file and >file 2>&1 do different things, because redirections are processed left to right. The second is the one that sends both to the file.

linux-text-processing.markdown:
## Why Text Processing Matters in DevOps

Linux systems expose a huge amount of information as plain text: logs, configuration files, command output, and status reports. That means DevOps engineers do not just read text; they filter it, search it, transform it, count it, and pipe it into other tools.

The commands in this lesson turn the shell into a lightweight data-processing environment.

## Searching with `grep`

`grep` searches for lines that match a pattern.

```bash
grep error app.log
grep -i failed app.log
grep -n timeout app.log
grep -r nginx /etc
```

Useful flags:

- `-i` ignores case
- `-n` shows line numbers
- `-r` searches recursively

### Basic Regular Expressions

`grep` supports regular expressions, which let you search by pattern instead of fixed text.

```bash
grep '^ERROR' app.log
grep '200$' access.log
grep '[0-9][0-9][0-9]' access.log
```

Examples:

- `^ERROR` means lines starting with `ERROR`
- `200$` means lines ending with `200`
- `[0-9]` matches a digit

> **Tip:** Start simple with fixed text, then add regex only when needed.

## Selecting Fields with `cut`

`cut` extracts parts of each line.

```bash
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd
cut -d' ' -f1 access.log
```

Here:

- `-d` sets the delimiter
- `-f` chooses the field number

For `/etc/passwd`, fields are separated by `:`. The first field is the username.

## Sorting and Deduplicating

`sort` orders lines. `uniq` removes adjacent duplicate lines.

```bash
sort names.txt
sort access.log | uniq
sort access.log | uniq -c
```

`uniq -c` also counts repeated entries.

This is helpful when summarizing logs or finding repeated values.

## Counting with `wc`

`wc` stands for **word count**, but it can count more than words.

```bash
wc app.log
wc -l app.log
wc -w notes.txt
wc -c payload.json
```

Useful flags:

- `-l` counts lines
- `-w` counts words
- `-c` counts bytes

Example use case:

```bash
grep ERROR app.log | wc -l
```

This counts how many error lines appear in the log.

## Pattern-Based Processing with `awk`

`awk` is a powerful text-processing language. For beginners, think of it as a tool for working with columns and applying logic.

```bash
awk '{print $1}' access.log
awk '/ERROR/ {print $0}' app.log
awk -F: '{print $1, $7}' /etc/passwd
```

Key ideas:

- `$1`, `$2`, `$3` refer to fields
- `-F:` sets the field separator to `:`
- `/pattern/ { action }` runs the action only on matching lines

A realistic example:

```bash
awk '$9 == 500 {print $1, $7}' access.log
```

In a typical web log, this might print client IPs and paths for HTTP 500 responses.

## Editing Streams with `sed`

`sed` is a stream editor. It is often used for quick substitutions.

```bash
sed 's/http:/https:/g' urls.txt
sed 's/DEBUG/INFO/g' app.log
```

The `s/old/new/g` pattern means substitute all matches on each line.

### In-Place Editing

You can modify a file directly with `-i`.

```bash
sed -i 's/listen 80/listen 8080/' nginx.conf
```

Be careful with in-place editing, especially on production configs.

> **Note:** It is often smart to copy a config file before running `sed -i` on it.

## Pipes and Redirection

A **pipe** sends the output of one command into another command.

```bash
cat access.log | grep 500 | wc -l
```

This works, but you can usually skip `cat` and write:

```bash
grep 500 access.log | wc -l
```

Redirection sends output to files.

```bash
grep ERROR app.log > errors.txt
grep WARN app.log >> errors.txt
command 2> error-output.txt
```

- `>` overwrites a file
- `>>` appends to a file
- `2>` redirects standard error

## A Real Log Analysis Workflow

Suppose you want to find the most common failing endpoint from a web log.

```bash
awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
```

This pipeline does four things:

1. selects lines with server errors
2. prints the request path
3. counts duplicates
4. sorts from highest count to lowest

That is a strong example of why text processing matters. You are turning raw logs into actionable insight with one command chain.

## When to Use Which Tool

- Use `grep` to find matching lines
- Use `cut` for simple field extraction
- Use `awk` for field logic and patterns
- Use `sed` for substitutions and quick edits
- Use `sort`, `uniq`, and `wc` for summarizing output

You do not need to master every advanced flag today. Learn the core use cases first, then build from there.

## Test Your Understanding

### Exercise 1: Anchoring a grep search

**Question:** If you want only log lines that begin with ERROR, which grep pattern from the lesson should you use?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-text-processing-q1',

    title: 'Exercise 1: Anchoring a grep search',

    description: 'Pick the grep pattern that matches lines starting with ERROR.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'grep \'200$\' app.log' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'grep \'[0-9][0-9][0-9]\' app.log' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'grep \'^ERROR\' app.log' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'grep -r /etc app.log' },

    ],

    correctId: 'c',

    explanation: 'The caret anchor means start of line, so ^ERROR finds lines whose first characters are ERROR. That is exactly the example the tutorial used to introduce simple regular expressions in grep.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: '200$ matches lines ending with 200, not lines beginning with ERROR.',

      b: 'This pattern finds any three digits in a row. It does not require the line to start with ERROR.',

      d: 'The -r flag controls recursive searching, but this command does not express the needed start-of-line pattern at all.',

    },

  }}
/>

### Exercise 2: Splitting fields with cut

**Question:** What does cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd return?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-text-processing-q2',

    title: 'Exercise 2: Splitting fields with cut',

    description: 'Determine what cut prints when it uses : as the delimiter and field 1.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'The first field from each colon-separated line, which is usually the username.' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'Only the first colon character found in the whole file.' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'The final field on each line, such as the login shell.' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'The file permissions for /etc/passwd.' },

    ],

    correctId: 'a',

    explanation: 'The lesson explains that -d sets the delimiter and -f selects the field number. In /etc/passwd, field 1 is the username, so this command is a simple way to list account names.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      b: 'cut operates line by line and prints fields, not individual delimiter characters.',

      c: 'Field 1 is the first field, not the last one. The shell path is farther to the right in each passwd entry.',

      d: 'Permissions come from commands like ls -l. cut just slices text fields from each line.',

    },

  }}
/>

### Exercise 3: Counting repeated values

**Scenario:** You want to know which HTTP path appears most often among 500-level responses.

**Question:** What is the main job of sort | uniq -c in the tutorial pipeline after awk prints the request path?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{

    id: 'linux-text-processing-q3',

    title: 'Exercise 3: Counting repeated values',

    description: 'Choose why sort and uniq -c are paired in the error-analysis pipeline.',

    options: [

      { id: 'a', text: 'They change every path into uppercase text before printing it.' },

      { id: 'b', text: 'They install a log parser package that understands HTTP status codes.' },

      { id: 'c', text: 'They group identical paths together and count how often each one appears.' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'They remove all duplicate lines without preserving any count information.' },

    ],

    correctId: 'c',

    explanation: 'The tutorial shows sort followed by uniq -c because uniq only counts adjacent duplicates. Sorting groups identical paths together first, and uniq -c then reports how many times each failing endpoint appeared.',

    wrongExplanations: {

      a: 'Neither sort nor uniq changes case here. They organize and count lines.',

      b: 'These are standard shell tools, not package installation commands.',

      d: 'uniq -c does preserve counts. The count is the point of using it in that pipeline.',

    },

  }}
/>

---

## Key takeaways

- **`grep` finds lines, `sed` edits them, `awk` works with fields.** Choose by what you need, not habit.
- **`grep -r "text" .` for a codebase** and `grep -c` when you only need the count.
- **`awk '{print $3}'` beats `cut` on whitespace**, because it treats runs of spaces as one separator.
- **`sed -i` edits in place**: and BSD sed on macOS requires an argument, so `sed -i ''` there and `sed -i` on Linux.
- **`sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`** is the log-analysis idiom worth memorising.
- **`uniq` only collapses adjacent duplicates**, so it is useless without sorting first.
- **`2>&1` merges stderr into stdout**; without it, piping silently drops your error messages.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**When should I use grep, sed or awk?**

`grep` selects lines matching a pattern and does nothing else. Reach for it when the question is "which lines". `sed` is a stream editor for substitution and deletion, so "change this to that" is its job, usually `sed 's/old/new/g'`. `awk` splits each line into fields and can do arithmetic and conditionals, so it wins whenever you care about columns, `awk '$3 > 100 {print $1}'`. If you find yourself building something with three pipes and a conditional, that is usually one `awk` program.

**How do I replace text in a file from the command line?**

`sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt`, `-i` edits in place, `s` substitutes, and `g` replaces every occurrence on each line rather than just the first. There is one portability trap: GNU sed on Linux accepts bare `-i`, while BSD sed on macOS requires a backup suffix, so the same command needs `sed -i '' 's/old/new/g'` there. Scripts that must run on both should use `perl -pi -e 's/old/new/g'`, which behaves identically everywhere.

**What is the difference between cut and awk for extracting columns?**

`cut -d' ' -f3` treats every single delimiter as a boundary, so two consecutive spaces produce an empty field, which makes it unreliable on command output aligned with variable whitespace. `awk '{print $3}'` treats any run of whitespace as one separator by default, which is almost always what you want for `ps`, `df` or log output. `cut` is the better tool for genuinely delimited data such as CSV or `/etc/passwd`, where the delimiter is exactly one character.

**How do I count unique occurrences in a log file?**

`sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`. The first `sort` is mandatory, because `uniq` only collapses *adjacent* duplicates and silently does nothing otherwise, that is the most common mistake with it. `uniq -c` prefixes each line with its count, and `sort -rn` orders by that count descending. Combined with `awk` to pull out a field, it answers most log questions: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` gives your top client IPs.

**How do I search recursively through a directory?**

`grep -rn "pattern" .`, `r` recurses, `n` adds line numbers so the output is actionable. Add `-i` for case-insensitive and `--include="*.py"` to limit by file type. `grep -rl` lists only the matching filenames, which is what you want when feeding results into another command. For large repositories, `ripgrep` (`rg`) is considerably faster and respects `.gitignore` by default, which usually removes more noise than any set of `--exclude` flags.

**Why does my error message disappear when I pipe a command?**

Because a pipe carries stdout only, and errors go to stderr. `command | grep error` therefore filters the normal output and lets the actual error print straight to your terminal, unfiltered. Redirect stderr into stdout first with `command 2>&1 | grep error`. The order matters: `2>&1 >file` and `>file 2>&1` do different things, because redirections are processed left to right. The second is the one that sends both to the file.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does chmod 755 mean?

Each digit is one class, user, group, other, and each is the sum of read (4), write (2) and execute (1). So 755 is rwxr-xr-x: the owner can read, write and execute; group and other can read and execute but not write. It is the standard mode for directories and for executable scripts. The other number you need is 644 (rw-r--r--), the standard for ordinary files, which is 755 without the execute bits.
What is the difference between chmod and chown?

chmod changes permissions. What the owner, group and everyone else are allowed to do. chown changes ownership, which user and group those permissions apply to. They solve different halves of the same problem, and picking the wrong one is a common source of frustration: if a service cannot write to its data directory, the fix is usually chown to the service's user rather than loosening the mode with chmod.
Why do permissions mean something different on a directory?

Because a directory is a list of names, not content. Read (r) lets you list what is inside; write (w) lets you create, rename and delete entries, which is why you can delete a file you cannot write to, as long as you can write to its directory. Execute (x) is the right to traverse the directory, to reach anything inside it. A directory with r but no x lets you see the file names and access none of them, which produces confusing "permission denied" errors on paths that clearly exist.
Is chmod 777 ever the right answer?

Effectively never. It makes a file readable, writable and executable by every account on the system, so any compromised process can rewrite it, and if it is a script something privileged runs, that is a direct path to privilege escalation. It is also usually treating the symptom: the real question is which user needs the access, answered with chown or by adding that user to the right group. The one defensible use is a deliberately shared scratch directory, and then it needs the sticky bit as well.
What are setuid, setgid and the sticky bit?

Three extra bits beyond rwx. setuid (chmod u+s) makes an executable run as its owner rather than the user invoking it. How /usr/bin/passwd can edit /etc/shadow on your behalf, and dangerous on anything else. setgid on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group, which is the clean way to share a folder between team members. The sticky bit (chmod +t) on a world-writable directory restricts deletion to each file's owner, which is why /tmp is safe to share.
How do umask and default permissions work?

umask is a mask of bits to remove from the defaults when a file is created: 666 for files and 777 for directories. The common default of 022 therefore yields 644 for files and 755 for directories. Set a stricter 077 and new files are readable only by you, which suits a multi-user server. Check the current value with umask and set it in ~/.bashrc for a user or /etc/profile for everyone; note that it affects only newly created files, not existing ones.
